cards.explanation: Eosinophils attach to worms too large to swallow and release cytotoxic granule proteins onto their surface. Basophils act in immediate allergic responses by releasing histamine. Neutrophils are aimed at bacteria and fungi and phagocytose particles small enough to engulf. Monocytes become macrophages that clean up debris and chronic infections.

cards.q: Which leukocyte gives rise to the plasma cells that secrete antibodies?
cards.a: The B lymphocyte.
options: The eosinophil
The monocyte
The B lymphocyte
The neutrophil
cards.explanation: Activated B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells, which are dedicated antibody factories, giving lymphocytes their role in specific humoral immunity. Neutrophils phagocytose bacteria but make no antibody. Eosinophils attack parasites with granule proteins. Monocytes become macrophages, which present antigen to lymphocytes but do not secrete antibody themselves.

cards.q: Which three leukocytes are classed as granulocytes?
cards.a: Neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.
options: Lymphocytes, monocytes, and neutrophils
Monocytes, eosinophils, and lymphocytes
Basophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes
Neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils
cards.explanation: These three carry conspicuous cytoplasmic granules whose contents define their function, from antibacterial enzymes to antiparasitic proteins to histamine. Lymphocytes and monocytes are agranulocytes with sparse granules and a large nucleus. Any grouping that includes a lymphocyte or a monocyte among the granulocytes mixes the two classes. The distinction matters because the granulocytes are short lived innate responders while the agranulocytes include the cells of specific immunity.

cards.q: What is the normal total leukocyte count in an adult?
cards.a: About 4,500 to 11,000 per microliter.
options: About 4,500 to 11,000 per microliter
About 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter
About 4.5 to 5.5 million per microliter
About 500 to 1,000 per microliter
cards.explanation: White cells are far outnumbered by red cells, sitting in the thousands per microliter, so a count above 11,000 suggests infection and one below 4,500 suggests marrow suppression. The 150,000 to 400,000 range is the platelet count. The millions per microliter range is the erythrocyte count. A count of 500 to 1,000 would be severe leukopenia with a serious risk of infection.

cards.q: What is leukopenia?
cards.a: An abnormally low white blood cell count.
options: An abnormally low red blood cell count
An abnormally low white blood cell count
An abnormally high white blood cell count
An abnormally low platelet count
cards.explanation: Leukopenia means too few defensive cells, most often from marrow suppression by drugs or radiation, and it leaves the patient vulnerable to infection. A high count is leukocytosis and usually signals infection or a marrow disorder. A low platelet count is thrombocytopenia, which causes bleeding rather than infection. A low red cell count is anemia and reduces oxygen delivery.

cards.q: A patient has acute appendicitis from a bacterial infection. Which leukocyte will be most elevated?
cards.a: Neutrophils.
options: Basophils
Lymphocytes
Neutrophils
Eosinophils
cards.explanation: Neutrophils are recruited within hours to bacterial sites and the marrow releases its reserve pool, so acute bacterial infection typically shows neutrophilia. Eosinophils rise with parasites and allergy, not with ordinary bacterial infection. Basophils are few in number and rise mainly with allergic and some chronic conditions. Lymphocytes lead the response to viral infection instead.

cards.q: A student has infectious mononucleosis, a viral illness. Which leukocyte pattern is expected?
cards.a: Lymphocytosis, an increase in lymphocytes.
options: Neutrophilia, an increase in neutrophils
Eosinophilia, an increase in eosinophils
Basophilia, an increase in basophils
Lymphocytosis, an increase in lymphocytes
cards.explanation: Viruses replicate inside host cells, so the response depends on lymphocytes that recognize infected cells and produce antibody, and their numbers climb. Neutrophils dominate bacterial infections and are often unremarkable or even reduced in viral illness. Eosinophils track parasites and allergy. Basophils are too scarce to define a response pattern.

cards.q: A patient with seasonal allergic rhinitis has a raised count of one leukocyte. Which one, and why?
cards.a: Eosinophils, because they are recruited in allergic and hypersensitivity responses.
options: Eosinophils, because they are recruited in allergic and hypersensitivity responses
Neutrophils, because allergens are treated as bacteria
Monocytes, because clearing allergens requires sustained phagocytosis by tissue macrophages
Lymphocytes, because allergens are viruses
cards.explanation: Eosinophils accumulate at sites of allergic inflammation, where they both contribute to and help limit the response, so an eosinophil count above the usual 2 to 4 percent points toward allergy or parasites. Allergens are not bacteria and do not drive a neutrophil response. Monocytes rise in chronic infections such as tuberculosis. Allergens are not viruses, so the lymphocyte pattern does not apply.

cards.q: A traveler returns with an intestinal roundworm infection. Which leukocyte count rises?
cards.a: The eosinophil count.
options: The monocyte count
The eosinophil count
The basophil count
The neutrophil count
cards.explanation: Worms are far too large to phagocytose, so the body sends eosinophils to coat them and release destructive granule proteins onto their surface, and the blood count rises markedly. Basophils act in immediate allergic reactions by releasing histamine. Neutrophils engulf bacteria and small particles. Monocytes and their macrophages handle chronic intracellular infections and tissue debris.

cards.q: A patient with chronic tuberculosis has a persistently elevated count of one leukocyte type. Which one, and why?
cards.a: Monocytes, because macrophages handle chronic intracellular infections.
options: Basophils, because chronic infection requires histamine release
Neutrophils, because chronic infection is simply prolonged acute infection
Monocytes, because macrophages handle chronic intracellular infections
Eosinophils, because mycobacteria are treated as parasites
cards.explanation: Mycobacteria survive inside cells, so the sustained response depends on monocytes entering tissue and becoming macrophages that wall the organism off in a granuloma, and blood monocytes rise. Mycobacteria are bacteria, not worms, so the eosinophil pathway does not apply. Histamine release is an immediate hypersensitivity mechanism, not a defense against chronic infection. Neutrophils dominate the first hours to days, but chronic infection recruits a different cell.

cards.q: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a white cell count of 1,200 per microliter. Predict the consequence.
cards.a: Marked vulnerability to infection, because too few defensive cells are available.
options: Excessive bleeding, because leukocytes are the cells that form the platelet plug and clot
Reduced oxygen delivery, because leukocytes carry oxygen
Jaundice, because leukocytes clear bilirubin
Marked vulnerability to infection, because too few defensive cells are available
cards.explanation: Chemotherapy suppresses rapidly dividing marrow precursors, and with the white count far below the normal 4,500 to 11,000 the patient cannot mount a normal response to bacteria or fungi. Bleeding comes from low platelets, which chemotherapy may also cause, but leukocytes themselves do not form the clot. Oxygen is carried by hemoglobin in red cells. Bilirubin is cleared by the liver, not by white cells.

cards.q: A differential count shows 88 percent neutrophils, many of them immature band forms, with a total white count of 19,000 per microliter. Interpret this.
cards.a: An acute bacterial infection driving the marrow to release immature neutrophils early.
options: An acute bacterial infection driving the marrow to release immature neutrophils early
A parasitic infection, since immature cells indicate worms
An allergic reaction, since a high total white cell count indicates a hypersensitivity response
A viral infection, since band forms are characteristic of viruses
cards.explanation: Two clues point the same way: the cell type is the bacterial responder, and the presence of immature bands means demand has outrun the mature reserve, a pattern often called a left shift. Parasitic infection would raise eosinophils rather than neutrophils. Allergy also raises eosinophils, and the total count alone does not identify a mechanism. Viral infection typically raises lymphocytes and does not produce a neutrophil left shift.

cards.q: Minutes after a bee sting, a patient develops widespread hives, itching, and a fall in blood pressure. Which leukocyte mediator explains this and how?
cards.a: Histamine from basophils and mast cells, which dilates arterioles and increases capillary permeability.
options: Heparin from eosinophils, which prevents clotting in the skin
Histamine from basophils and mast cells, which dilates arterioles and leaks capillary fluid
Lysozyme from neutrophils, which digests bacterial cell walls
Antibody from plasma cells, which binds the venom but takes several days to be produced in quantity
cards.explanation: Histamine acts within minutes, widening arterioles so blood pressure falls and loosening capillary junctions so fluid leaks into skin as wheals, which matches the speed and the signs. Lysozyme is antibacterial and would not cause vasodilation. Antibody production does take days, so it cannot explain a reaction that begins in minutes, although preformed IgE is what triggered the release. Heparin comes from basophils and mast cells rather than eosinophils, and anticoagulation does not produce hives.

cards.q: Untreated HIV infection progressively destroys helper T lymphocytes. Predict the consequence for defense and explain why.
cards.a: Opportunistic infections increase, because helper T cells coordinate both antibody production and cell mediated defense.
options: Anemia is the first consequence, because lymphocytes carry oxygen
Allergic reactions disappear, because all leukocyte function is lost
Opportunistic infections increase, because helper T cells coordinate antibody and cell mediated defense
Bleeding increases, because helper T lymphocytes are required for platelet plug formation and clotting
cards.explanation: Helper T cells sit at the center of specific immunity, activating B cells and cytotoxic T cells, so their loss disables far more than their own numbers suggest and organisms that a healthy person contains become dangerous. Platelet plug formation depends on platelets and von Willebrand factor, not on lymphocytes. Lymphocytes do not carry oxygen; that is the red cell's job. Other leukocyte lines persist, so defense is impaired selectively rather than abolished across the board.

cards.q: Two patients each have a total white count of 14,000 per microliter. Patient A has 82 percent neutrophils and patient B has 38 percent eosinophils. What does the differential add that the total does not?
cards.a: It identifies the kind of threat, pointing to bacterial infection in A and to parasites or allergy in B.
options: It measures how severe the infection is, showing B is sicker than A
It shows which patient is anemic, since a high eosinophil share reduces hemoglobin production in the marrow
It adds nothing, since both totals are identical
It identifies the kind of threat, pointing to bacterial infection in A and to parasites or allergy in B
cards.explanation: The total says only that the immune system is mobilized, while the proportions say which arm is mobilized, and each cell line is tied to a characteristic class of threat. Severity is not read from the differential percentages, and a higher eosinophil share does not mean a sicker patient. Eosinophils have no effect on hemoglobin concentration. The two counts are identical, which is exactly why the differential is the informative test.

cards.q: What is the first phase of hemostasis after a vessel is cut?
cards.a: Vascular spasm.
options: Vascular spasm
Platelet plug formation
Coagulation
Fibrinolysis
cards.explanation: Injury makes the vessel wall smooth muscle contract immediately, narrowing the lumen and cutting blood loss before anything else has time to happen. Platelet plug formation comes second, once collagen is exposed and platelets can adhere. Coagulation is third and builds the fibrin mesh that stabilizes the plug. Fibrinolysis is the later removal of the clot, not part of the three phases of stopping bleeding.

cards.q: What is the correct order of the three phases of hemostasis?
cards.a: Vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, coagulation.
options: Vascular spasm, coagulation, platelet plug formation
Vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, coagulation
Platelet plug formation, vascular spasm, coagulation
Coagulation, vascular spasm, platelet plug formation
cards.explanation: Each phase buys time for the next: spasm reduces flow in seconds, the platelet plug seals small breaks in a minute or two, and coagulation reinforces the plug with fibrin over several minutes. Starting with the platelet plug skips the immediate muscular response. Coagulation cannot come first because it needs a platelet surface and exposed tissue factor to get going. Putting coagulation before the platelet plug reverses the scaffold and the reinforcement.

cards.q: What does von Willebrand factor do?
cards.a: It bridges platelets to collagen exposed in the damaged vessel wall.
options: It causes vascular smooth muscle to relax
It dissolves the fibrin strands of the clot once healing is complete
It bridges platelets to collagen exposed in the damaged vessel wall
It converts fibrinogen into fibrin
cards.explanation: Von Willebrand factor is a large adhesive protein that grips subendothelial collagen at one end and a platelet surface receptor at the other, making adhesion possible under flowing blood. Converting fibrinogen to fibrin is the job of thrombin. Relaxing vascular smooth muscle is the opposite of what injury calls for and describes nitric oxide. Dissolving fibrin is the work of plasmin during fibrinolysis.

cards.q: What does thromboxane A2 released by activated platelets do?
cards.a: It promotes platelet aggregation and constricts the vessel.
options: It inhibits platelet aggregation and dilates the vessel
It converts prothrombin into thrombin
It cross links fibrin strands
It promotes platelet aggregation and constricts the vessel
cards.explanation: Thromboxane A2 is made from arachidonic acid by cyclooxygenase in the platelet and does two pro hemostatic jobs at once, recruiting more platelets and narrowing the vessel. Inhibiting aggregation and dilating the vessel describes prostacyclin, the endothelial counterpart that keeps the plug from spreading. Converting prothrombin to thrombin is done by factor Xa in the common pathway. Cross linking fibrin is the job of factor XIII.

cards.q: Platelets are fragments shed from which marrow cell?
cards.a: The megakaryocyte.
options: The megakaryocyte
The reticulocyte
The monocyte
The myeloblast
cards.explanation: Megakaryocytes are enormous multilobed marrow cells whose cytoplasm pinches off into thousands of anucleate platelets. A reticulocyte is a young red cell. A monocyte is a leukocyte that becomes a macrophage. A myeloblast is the granulocyte precursor and gives rise to neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.

cards.q: What is the normal platelet count in an adult?
cards.a: About 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter.
options: About 15,000 to 40,000 per microliter
About 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter
About 4,500 to 11,000 per microliter
About 4.5 to 5.5 million per microliter
cards.explanation: Platelets are far more numerous than white cells but far fewer than red cells, and counts below about 50,000 begin to threaten hemostasis. The 4,500 to 11,000 range is the total leukocyte count. The millions per microliter range is the erythrocyte count. A count of 15,000 to 40,000 would be severe thrombocytopenia with a real risk of spontaneous bleeding.

cards.q: Which substance released from platelet granules recruits additional platelets to the growing plug?
cards.a: ADP.
options: Nitric oxide
Plasminogen
ADP
Prostacyclin
cards.explanation: Platelets release ADP from dense granules, and it activates passing platelets so they in turn release more, a positive feedback loop that builds the plug quickly. Prostacyclin comes from intact endothelium and inhibits aggregation. Nitric oxide also comes from endothelium and both dilates the vessel and discourages platelet adhesion. Plasminogen is the inactive precursor of the enzyme that later dissolves the clot.

cards.q: What does intact endothelium release to keep platelets from sticking where there is no injury?
cards.a: Prostacyclin and nitric oxide.
options: Thromboxane A2 and ADP
Von Willebrand factor and collagen
Thrombin and fibrinogen
Prostacyclin and nitric oxide
cards.explanation: Healthy endothelium continuously produces these two inhibitors, so platelets glide past undamaged wall and the plug stays confined to the injury. Thromboxane A2 and ADP are the platelet derived signals that do the opposite, promoting aggregation. Von Willebrand factor and collagen are adhesive surfaces exposed by injury, not inhibitors. Thrombin and fibrinogen drive the coagulation phase.

cards.q: A patient inherits a deficiency of von Willebrand factor. Predict the effect on hemostasis.
cards.a: Platelet adhesion to collagen fails, so the plug forms poorly and bleeding time is prolonged.
options: Platelet adhesion to collagen fails, so the plug forms poorly and bleeding time is prolonged
Platelet count falls well below normal, so there are too few platelets left to form a plug at all
Fibrin cannot be cross linked, so the clot dissolves as soon as it forms
Vascular spasm fails, so the vessel cannot narrow after injury
cards.explanation: Without the bridging protein, platelets cannot grab exposed collagen against the shear of flowing blood, so the very first step of plug formation is defective even though the platelets themselves are normal. The platelet count is typically normal in this disorder, which is the clue that separates it from thrombocytopenia. Cross linking is factor XIII work and is unaffected. Vascular spasm depends on smooth muscle and does not require von Willebrand factor.

cards.q: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase in platelets. Predict the effect on hemostasis.
cards.a: Less thromboxane A2 is made, so platelet aggregation is reduced and bleeding time lengthens.
options: More von Willebrand factor is made, so adhesion increases
Less thromboxane A2 is made, so platelet aggregation is reduced and bleeding time lengthens
Less thrombin is made, so fibrin formation is reduced
Fewer platelets are produced in the marrow, so the circulating platelet count falls steadily
cards.explanation: Cyclooxygenase is the enzyme that makes thromboxane A2 from arachidonic acid, so blocking it removes one of the main recruitment signals and the plug builds more slowly. Thrombin generation belongs to the coagulation cascade and is not affected by aspirin, which is why prothrombin time stays normal. Aspirin acts on platelet function, not on marrow production, so the count is unchanged. Von Willebrand factor synthesis is endothelial and is not increased by aspirin.

cards.q: Why is platelet plug formation described as a positive feedback process?
cards.a: Activated platelets release ADP and thromboxane A2, which activate more platelets, which release more of the same.
options: Thrombin destroys platelets, which limits the size of the plug
Each platelet divides once it adheres, doubling the number present
Activated platelets release ADP and thromboxane A2, which activate still more platelets
The plug releases prostacyclin, which recruits still more platelets until the vessel is fully sealed
cards.explanation: The output of the process amplifies its own input, which is the definition of positive feedback and is why a plug forms explosively at the injury site. Prostacyclin does the opposite, inhibiting aggregation, and it comes from endothelium rather than the plug. Thrombin actually activates platelets rather than destroying them. Platelets are anucleate cell fragments and cannot divide.

cards.q: A patient's platelet count is 20,000 per microliter. What clinical sign would you expect?
cards.a: Pinpoint hemorrhages in the skin, because tiny vessel breaks are not sealed.
options: Widespread clotting in small vessels, because fewer platelets clot faster
Prolonged vascular spasm, because platelets normally inhibit smooth muscle
No abnormality, because coagulation factors compensate fully
Pinpoint hemorrhages in the skin, because tiny vessel breaks are not sealed
cards.explanation: Everyday minor capillary damage is normally patched by platelets alone, so when they are scarce the small leaks show up as petechiae and easy bruising. Fewer platelets cannot cause more clotting. Platelets promote vasoconstriction through thromboxane and serotonin, so losing them does not prolong spasm. Coagulation factors need a platelet surface to work efficiently and cannot substitute for the plug.

cards.q: What exposed material in the vessel wall triggers platelet adhesion?
cards.a: Subendothelial collagen.
options: Subendothelial collagen
Prostacyclin
Fibrin
Elastin in the tunica media
cards.explanation: Endothelium normally hides the collagen underneath it, so a break uncovers a surface that von Willebrand factor and platelet receptors bind avidly, marking the exact site of injury. Prostacyclin is an endothelial inhibitor of adhesion, the opposite signal. Fibrin appears later, after coagulation has been triggered, so it is a consequence and not the trigger. Elastin gives the vessel recoil but is not the adhesion signal.

cards.q: How does vascular spasm reduce blood loss?
cards.a: Smooth muscle contraction narrows the lumen, lowering flow through the injured segment.
options: Systemic blood pressure falls throughout the body, so much less blood reaches the wound
Smooth muscle contraction narrows the lumen, lowering flow through the injured segment
The endothelium secretes fibrin that plugs the tear directly
Blood viscosity rises sharply so flow slows
cards.explanation: Narrowing the vessel raises resistance locally, and because flow falls steeply as radius shrinks, even a modest constriction cuts loss substantially and gives platelets a slower stream to work in. Endothelium does not secrete fibrin; fibrin comes from plasma fibrinogen acted on by thrombin. Viscosity does not change appreciably in the seconds after injury. A systemic pressure drop would be a sign of serious blood loss rather than a local protective mechanism.

cards.q: Why is a platelet plug alone insufficient to stop bleeding from a larger vessel?
cards.a: It is loose and unreinforced, so it needs a fibrin mesh to withstand the pressure and flow.
options: It dissolves immediately because plasmin is always active
It cannot form at all when flow velocity is high
It is loose and unreinforced, so it needs a fibrin mesh to withstand the pressure
It contains no platelets capable of adhering to the exposed collagen of a large vessel
cards.explanation: The plug is an aggregate of sticky cell fragments and can be washed away by the higher pressure and shear in a larger vessel until fibrin strands lock it in place, which is exactly why the third phase exists. The same adhesion machinery works in vessels of all sizes. Plasmin is generated locally and gradually rather than being constantly active enough to strip fresh plugs. Plugs do form under high shear; von Willebrand factor is specifically adapted for that condition.

cards.q: A patient taking daily aspirin cuts a finger and it oozes for much longer than usual, but a laboratory test of the coagulation cascade is normal. Trace the mechanism.
cards.a: Cyclooxygenase is blocked, thromboxane A2 falls, platelet recruitment falls, the plug forms slowly, but fibrin generation is untouched.
options: Vitamin K is blocked, prothrombin falls, fibrin generation falls, and the platelet phase is left untouched
Von Willebrand factor is destroyed, adhesion fails, and the cascade is also impaired
Platelet production in the marrow is suppressed, so the count falls and the cascade slows
Cyclooxygenase is blocked, thromboxane A2 falls, platelet recruitment falls, and the plug forms slowly
cards.explanation: Aspirin acts only on the platelet arm, so the phase that seals small cuts is impaired while the enzymes that make fibrin work normally, which is why the cascade test comes back normal. Blocking vitamin K describes warfarin and would prolong the cascade test, contradicting the finding. Aspirin does not affect von Willebrand factor, and the cascade is specifically spared here. Aspirin does not suppress marrow production, so the platelet count is normal.

cards.q: A patient with von Willebrand disease has a normal platelet count but prolonged bleeding after dental work, and a mildly prolonged cascade test as well. Explain both findings.
cards.a: Adhesion fails because the bridging protein is missing, and factor VIII is less stable because von Willebrand factor normally carries it.
options: Adhesion fails because the bridging protein is missing, and factor VIII is less stable without it
Platelets are destroyed in the spleen, and the cascade slows because platelets are the source of all clotting factors
Fibrinogen is absent, so both the plug and the fibrin mesh fail
Vitamin K is deficient, so adhesion and the cascade both fail
cards.explanation: Von Willebrand factor has two jobs, gluing platelets to collagen and chaperoning factor VIII in the plasma, so a deficiency shows up in both the platelet phase and, more mildly, the intrinsic cascade. Splenic destruction would lower the platelet count, which is stated to be normal. Absent fibrinogen would cause a far more severe cascade defect and would not spare the count either. Vitamin K deficiency affects the cascade only and has no effect on platelet adhesion.

cards.q: Patient A has a platelet count of 15,000 per microliter. Patient B has normal platelets but a severe clotting factor deficiency. How do their bleeding patterns differ?
cards.a: Patient A shows petechiae and mucosal oozing, while patient B shows deep bleeding into joints and muscles.
options: Neither bleeds abnormally, because vascular spasm compensates
Patient A shows petechiae and mucosal oozing, while patient B shows deep joint bleeding
Patient A shows deep bleeding into joints and muscles, while patient B shows petechiae and oozing
Both show identical patterns, since both phases end in the same clot
cards.explanation: Platelets patch the constant small capillary breaks in skin and mucosa, so losing them gives many tiny surface bleeds, while fibrin holds together the larger clots needed in deep tissue, so losing factors gives fewer but larger and deeper hemorrhages. The pattern is not reversed; joint bleeding is the hallmark of factor deficiency such as hemophilia. The two phases do different jobs, so the patterns differ. Vascular spasm lasts only seconds to minutes and cannot compensate for either defect.

cards.q: Put the events after a small skin cut in the correct order: fibrin mesh traps cells, platelets adhere to collagen through von Willebrand factor, smooth muscle contracts, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets.
cards.a: Smooth muscle contracts, platelets adhere through von Willebrand factor, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets, fibrin mesh traps cells.
options: Fibrin mesh traps cells, smooth muscle contracts, platelets adhere through von Willebrand factor, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets
Smooth muscle contracts, fibrin mesh traps cells, platelets adhere through von Willebrand factor, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets
Smooth muscle contracts, platelets adhere through von Willebrand factor, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets, fibrin mesh traps cells
Platelets adhere through von Willebrand factor, smooth muscle contracts, fibrin mesh traps cells, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets
cards.explanation: The sequence follows the three phases: an immediate muscular response, then adhesion, then amplification that builds the plug, and finally the fibrin reinforcement that turns the plug into a clot. Adhesion cannot precede the spasm, which begins within seconds of injury. Fibrin cannot come first, because coagulation requires the platelet surface and exposed tissue factor. Putting fibrin before adhesion places the reinforcement before the structure it reinforces.

cards.q: What initiates the extrinsic pathway of coagulation?
cards.a: Tissue factor released from damaged tissue outside the vessel.
options: Contact of factor XII with the collagen exposed in the injured vessel wall
Thrombin acting on fibrinogen
Calcium binding to platelet membranes
Tissue factor released from damaged tissue outside the vessel
cards.explanation: Tissue factor, also called factor III, is a membrane protein of cells outside the bloodstream, so it meets blood only when tissue is injured, and it activates factor VII to start the fast pathway. Contact activation of factor XII starts the intrinsic pathway instead. Thrombin acting on fibrinogen is the end of the common pathway, not the beginning. Calcium is required at several steps but is not the initiating signal.

cards.q: What initiates the intrinsic pathway of coagulation?
cards.a: Contact of factor XII with a negatively charged surface such as exposed collagen.
options: Contact of factor XII with a negatively charged surface such as exposed collagen
Release of tissue factor from injured cells in the tissues just outside the vessel
Conversion of prothrombin to thrombin
Cross linking of fibrin by factor XIII
cards.explanation: The intrinsic pathway uses only components already present in blood, and it begins when factor XII contacts a charged surface such as collagen or glass, which is why blood clots in a plain glass tube. Tissue factor starts the extrinsic pathway, which requires something from outside the blood. Prothrombin conversion is a common pathway step downstream of both. Cross linking is the last step of all, after fibrin has already formed.

cards.q: At which factor do the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge?
cards.a: Factor X.
options: Factor XIII
Factor X
Factor VII
Factor XII
cards.explanation: Both pathways end by activating factor X, and from there a single common pathway runs to thrombin and fibrin. Factor VII belongs only to the extrinsic pathway. Factor XII belongs only to the intrinsic pathway. Factor XIII acts after fibrin has formed and is the final stabilizing step rather than the convergence point.

cards.q: What reaction does thrombin catalyze?
cards.a: It converts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin monomers.
options: It converts plasminogen into plasmin
It converts factor X into tissue factor
It converts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin monomers
It converts prothrombin into fibrinogen in the plasma
cards.explanation: Thrombin is a protease that clips fibrinogen so the pieces polymerize into insoluble strands, which is the defining event of clot formation. Prothrombin is thrombin's own precursor, and fibrinogen is a separate protein made by the liver. Converting plasminogen to plasmin is done by tissue plasminogen activator during clot removal. Factor X is activated to Xa upstream of thrombin and is never converted into tissue factor.

cards.q: Which clotting factor is prothrombin?
cards.a: Factor II.
options: Factor I
Factor III
Factor X
Factor II
cards.explanation: Prothrombin is factor II, the circulating precursor that factor Xa cleaves into active thrombin. Factor I is fibrinogen, the substrate that thrombin acts on. Factor III is tissue factor, the trigger of the extrinsic pathway. Factor X is the convergence point whose active form generates thrombin.

cards.q: What role does calcium play in coagulation?
cards.a: It is required as a cofactor at several steps of both pathways.
options: It is required as a cofactor at several steps of both pathways
It is the substrate that thrombin converts into fibrin
It dissolves the clot once healing is complete
It is the surface receptor that binds tissue factor
cards.explanation: Calcium, listed as factor IV, tethers vitamin K dependent factors to phospholipid surfaces so the reactions can proceed, which is why removing calcium from a blood sample prevents clotting. Fibrinogen, not calcium, is thrombin's substrate. Clot dissolution is performed by plasmin. Tissue factor is itself a membrane protein and does not need a calcium receptor to be recognized.

cards.q: Which clotting factors require vitamin K for their synthesis in the liver?
cards.a: Factors II, VII, IX, and X.
options: Factors V, VI, VIII, and XI
Factors II, VII, IX, and X
Factors I, V, VIII, and XIII
Factors III, IV, XI, and XII
cards.explanation: Vitamin K is the cofactor for the enzyme that adds calcium binding sites to these four factors, plus the regulatory proteins C and S, so a deficiency cripples both pathways at once. Factor I is fibrinogen and factor XIII is the cross linker, and neither is vitamin K dependent. Factor III is tissue factor and factor IV is calcium, neither of which is synthesized as a vitamin K dependent protein. Factors V, VIII and XI are made in the liver but do not require vitamin K.

cards.q: What does factor XIII do?
cards.a: It cross links fibrin strands to stabilize the clot.
options: It activates factor X in the common pathway
It digests fibrin during clot removal
It cross links fibrin strands to stabilize the clot
It converts prothrombin into thrombin
cards.explanation: Fibrin monomers first polymerize into a fragile mesh, and factor XIIIa forms covalent bonds between them so the clot resists mechanical stress and premature dissolution. Prothrombin conversion is carried out by factor Xa with factor V as cofactor. Factor X is activated by the ends of the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways. Digesting fibrin is the work of plasmin, which acts against factor XIII's product.

cards.q: Which pathway generates fibrin faster after a traumatic injury, and why?
cards.a: The extrinsic pathway, because it takes fewer steps to reach factor X.
options: The intrinsic pathway, because it needs no external trigger
The extrinsic pathway, because it does not require calcium
The intrinsic pathway, because factor XII is the most abundant factor
The extrinsic pathway, because it takes fewer steps to reach factor X
cards.explanation: Tissue factor plus factor VII activates factor X almost directly, so fibrin appears in about fifteen seconds, while the intrinsic pathway needs a longer chain of activations and takes several minutes. Needing no external trigger does not make a pathway faster; it makes it slower here because more steps are involved. Both pathways require calcium. Abundance of a factor does not determine the speed of the sequence.

cards.q: A blood sample is collected in a tube containing citrate, which binds calcium. Why does the sample not clot?
cards.a: Calcium is required as a cofactor at multiple steps, so the cascade cannot proceed.
options: Calcium is required as a cofactor at multiple steps, so the cascade cannot proceed
Citrate destroys fibrinogen so there is no substrate for thrombin
Citrate blocks vitamin K, so no factors are synthesized in the tube
Citrate inactivates platelets, and platelets are the only source of clotting factors
cards.explanation: Chelating calcium removes the ion that anchors several factors to phospholipid surfaces, so both pathways stall, and adding calcium back lets the sample clot. Fibrinogen remains intact in a citrated tube, which is why fibrinogen can be measured from it. Vitamin K acts during synthesis in the liver, and no synthesis is happening in a collection tube. Platelets are affected by the lack of calcium too, but clotting factors are plasma proteins made by the liver, not by platelets.

cards.q: A patient has a vitamin K deficiency from prolonged antibiotic use and poor diet. Predict the effect on coagulation.
cards.a: Both pathways slow, because four factors including prothrombin are made in nonfunctional form.
options: Coagulation speeds up, because vitamin K normally inhibits the cascade
Both pathways slow, because four factors including prothrombin are made in nonfunctional form
Only the intrinsic pathway slows, because vitamin K acts on factor XII
Only fibrin cross linking fails, because vitamin K is required for the activity of factor XIII
cards.explanation: Factors II, VII, IX and X span the extrinsic, intrinsic and common pathways, so a vitamin K shortage lengthens both routes to fibrin. Factor XII is not vitamin K dependent, so the effect is not limited to the intrinsic side. Factor XIII does not require vitamin K either. Vitamin K enables rather than inhibits factor synthesis, so its absence slows clotting rather than speeding it.

cards.q: Thrombin activates factors V, VIII, and XI in addition to cleaving fibrinogen. What does this accomplish?
cards.a: It creates positive feedback that accelerates its own production once clotting has begun.
options: It converts the intrinsic pathway into the extrinsic pathway
It replaces the need for calcium in the common pathway
It creates positive feedback that accelerates its own production once clotting has begun
It creates negative feedback that shuts the whole cascade down long before fibrin can form
cards.explanation: Thrombin amplifying the steps that make more thrombin is a classic positive feedback loop and explains why fibrin formation accelerates sharply once it starts. Negative feedback would slow the cascade, which is instead the job of antithrombin and protein C. Thrombin does not convert one pathway into another; the two pathways keep their own triggers. Calcium remains necessary regardless of thrombin's amplifying actions.

cards.q: A patient with advanced liver disease bleeds easily. What is the mechanism?
cards.a: The liver synthesizes most clotting factors, so factor levels fall.
options: The liver stores platelets, so the platelet count falls to zero
The liver produces calcium for the cascade, so calcium falls
The liver secretes plasmin, so clots dissolve too fast
The liver synthesizes most clotting factors, so factor levels fall
cards.explanation: Fibrinogen, prothrombin and nearly every other factor are hepatocyte products, so failing liver tissue reduces the supply and the cascade runs short of substrate. The spleen, not the liver, sequesters platelets, and the count falls but not to zero. Plasma calcium is regulated by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D, not by liver synthesis. Plasmin is generated from plasminogen by tissue plasminogen activator, and the liver actually makes plasminogen rather than secreting active plasmin.

cards.q: Which laboratory test evaluates the extrinsic and common pathways?
cards.a: The prothrombin time.
options: The prothrombin time
The activated partial thromboplastin time
The bleeding time
The platelet count
cards.explanation: Prothrombin time is run by adding tissue factor to plasma, so it measures how fast the extrinsic route reaches fibrin and is the test that responds to warfarin and to factor VII deficiency. The activated partial thromboplastin time uses a contact activator and tests the intrinsic and common pathways instead. Bleeding time assesses platelet function rather than the cascade. The platelet count is a number of cells and says nothing about factor activity.

cards.q: Hemophilia A is a deficiency of factor VIII. Which pathway is affected and what happens to the laboratory tests?
cards.a: The intrinsic pathway, so the partial thromboplastin time is prolonged while the prothrombin time is normal.
options: Neither pathway, so both tests are normal and only bleeding time is prolonged
The intrinsic pathway, so the partial thromboplastin time is prolonged while the prothrombin time is normal
The extrinsic pathway, so the prothrombin time is prolonged while the partial thromboplastin time is normal
The common pathway, so both tests are prolonged equally
cards.explanation: Factor VIII is the cofactor for factor IXa in the intrinsic route, so only the test that runs through that route is prolonged, and the pattern of one abnormal test localizes the defect. The extrinsic pathway does not use factor VIII, so prothrombin time is spared. A common pathway defect such as low factor X or prothrombin would prolong both. Bleeding time reflects platelet function, which is normal in hemophilia.

cards.q: A patient has a prolonged prothrombin time with a normal partial thromboplastin time. Where is the defect?
cards.a: In the extrinsic pathway, most likely factor VII.
options: In the common pathway, most likely factor X
In platelet function, most likely von Willebrand factor
In the extrinsic pathway, most likely factor VII
In the intrinsic pathway, most likely factor VIII
cards.explanation: Only one test is abnormal, so the defect must lie in a factor unique to that pathway, and factor VII is the only factor tested exclusively by prothrombin time. A factor VIII problem would prolong the partial thromboplastin time instead, since factor VIII is unique to the intrinsic route. A common pathway defect would prolong both tests, because both routes pass through it. Platelet defects do not lengthen either cascade test.

cards.q: Newborns are given vitamin K at birth. Explain the physiology behind this.
cards.a: Vitamin K crosses the placenta poorly and the newborn gut is not yet colonized by bacteria that make it, so factors II, VII, IX, and X are low.
options: Newborns have no platelets until the second week, so vitamin K substitutes for them
Newborn liver cannot make fibrinogen, and vitamin K is converted into fibrinogen
Vitamin K is needed to break down fetal hemoglobin, which otherwise blocks the clotting cascade completely
Vitamin K crosses the placenta poorly and the newborn gut is not yet colonized by bacteria that make it
cards.explanation: Two supply routes are missing at once, maternal transfer and gut bacterial synthesis, so the four vitamin K dependent factors are made in inactive form and bleeding risk is real until feeding establishes the gut flora. Newborns do have normal platelet counts, and vitamin K cannot substitute for platelets in any case. Fibrinogen is not made from vitamin K and is not vitamin K dependent. Fetal hemoglobin has no role in coagulation.

cards.q: Plasma from a citrated tube is warmed and calcium is added back. Predict what happens and why.
cards.a: It clots, because the only missing element was the calcium cofactor and all the factors are still present.
options: It clots, because the only missing element was calcium and all the factors are still present
It does not clot, because citrate permanently destroys the clotting factors
It does not clot, because plasma has no platelets and platelets make the factors
It clots only if vitamin K is also added, because vitamin K acts directly in the cascade reactions
cards.explanation: Citrate works by sequestering calcium, a reversible chemical effect, so restoring calcium restores the surface binding steps and the cascade proceeds, which is the basis of standard coagulation testing. Citrate does not damage the protein factors themselves. Clotting factors are plasma proteins made by the liver, so platelet free plasma still clots, though less efficiently without a platelet surface. Vitamin K acts during hepatic synthesis, not in the reaction tube.

cards.q: Trace the extrinsic pathway from injury to a stabilized clot in the correct order.
cards.a: Tissue factor activates factor VII, factor VIIa activates factor X, factor Xa converts prothrombin to thrombin, thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, factor XIIIa cross links the fibrin.
options: Prothrombin activates tissue factor, tissue factor activates factor X, factor Xa converts fibrin to fibrinogen, and factor XIIIa dissolves the finished clot
Tissue factor activates factor VII, factor VIIa activates factor X, factor Xa makes thrombin, thrombin makes fibrin, factor XIIIa cross links it
Factor XII activates factor VII, factor VIIa converts fibrinogen to thrombin, thrombin activates factor X, factor X cross links fibrin
Tissue factor converts fibrinogen to fibrin, fibrin activates factor X, factor Xa activates thrombin, thrombin cross links the clot
cards.explanation: The order follows the logic of a cascade: an external trigger, a short extrinsic segment, convergence at factor X, thrombin generation, fibrin formation, and finally stabilization. Factor XII belongs to the intrinsic pathway and does not activate factor VII. Tissue factor cannot act on fibrinogen directly, since only thrombin does that. The last option reverses several steps, including turning fibrin back into fibrinogen and having factor XIII dissolve rather than stabilize the clot.

cards.q: Which enzyme digests the fibrin mesh of a clot?
cards.a: Plasmin.
options: Factor XIIIa
Carbonic anhydrase
Plasmin
Thrombin
cards.explanation: Plasmin is a protease that cleaves fibrin into soluble fragments, gradually dismantling the clot as the vessel heals. Thrombin does the opposite, generating fibrin from fibrinogen. Factor XIIIa strengthens fibrin by cross linking it. Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the reaction between carbon dioxide and water and has no role in clotting.

cards.q: What is the inactive precursor of plasmin?
cards.a: Plasminogen.
options: Prothrombin
Fibrinogen
Prekallikrein
Plasminogen
cards.explanation: Plasminogen circulates inactive and is trapped inside the clot as it forms, so the tool for taking the clot apart is built into the clot itself. Prothrombin is the precursor of thrombin, which builds the clot. Fibrinogen is the precursor of fibrin, the clot's structural protein. Prekallikrein participates in contact activation of the intrinsic pathway rather than in fibrinolysis.

cards.q: What converts plasminogen into plasmin?
cards.a: Tissue plasminogen activator.
options: Tissue plasminogen activator
Thrombin acting alone
Factor XII acting alone
Antithrombin III bound to heparin
cards.explanation: Endothelial cells release tissue plasminogen activator, which cleaves plasminogen bound within the clot, keeping fibrinolysis local. Thrombin contributes indirectly to fibrinolysis but its main action is making fibrin, not plasmin. Factor XII has a minor role in activating the system but is not the principal activator. Antithrombin III inactivates thrombin and other proteases rather than generating plasmin.

cards.q: What does antithrombin III do?
cards.a: It inactivates thrombin and several other activated clotting factors.
options: It carries factor VIII through the plasma
It inactivates thrombin and several other activated clotting factors
It converts plasminogen into plasmin
It cross links the fibrin strands to stabilize and harden the finished clot
cards.explanation: Antithrombin III binds and neutralizes thrombin and factors such as Xa, keeping coagulation from spreading beyond the injury, and heparin accelerates its action dramatically. Generating plasmin is the job of tissue plasminogen activator. Cross linking fibrin is done by factor XIIIa. Carrying factor VIII is one of the functions of von Willebrand factor.

cards.q: Which cells are the natural source of heparin in the body?
cards.a: Basophils and mast cells.
options: Hepatocytes
Endothelial cells only
Basophils and mast cells
Platelets
cards.explanation: Heparin is stored in the granules of basophils and their tissue counterparts, mast cells, and released during inflammation to discourage clotting locally. Platelets release ADP, serotonin and thromboxane, which promote clotting rather than prevent it. The liver makes clotting factors and plasminogen, not heparin. Endothelium contributes heparan sulfate and other anticoagulant surfaces, but it is not the source usually named for heparin itself.

cards.q: How does warfarin reduce clotting?
cards.a: It blocks the recycling of vitamin K, so the liver makes nonfunctional factors II, VII, IX, and X.
options: It binds the calcium in the plasma so that the cascade reactions cannot proceed at all
It blocks cyclooxygenase so platelets cannot aggregate
It activates plasmin so existing clots are dissolved
It blocks the recycling of vitamin K, so factors II, VII, IX, and X are nonfunctional
cards.explanation: Warfarin inhibits the enzyme that regenerates active vitamin K, so newly synthesized factors lack their calcium binding sites and cannot work, which is why the effect takes days to appear. Binding calcium in plasma is how citrate works in a test tube, and it would be lethal in the body. Blocking cyclooxygenase describes aspirin, which acts on platelets rather than factors. Warfarin does not dissolve clots already present; that is the action of tissue plasminogen activator.

cards.q: What is D-dimer?
cards.a: A fibrin degradation fragment produced when plasmin digests a cross linked clot.
options: A fibrin degradation fragment produced when plasmin digests a cross linked clot
The activated form of fibrinogen produced just before it polymerizes into strands
The complex of heparin and antithrombin III
The storage form of vitamin K in the liver
cards.explanation: Because it comes only from fibrin that was already cross linked by factor XIII, a raised D-dimer means a clot formed somewhere and is being broken down. Fibrinogen before polymerization is simply fibrinogen. The heparin and antithrombin complex is an anticoagulant mechanism and is not the measured fragment. Vitamin K is stored in the liver as the vitamin itself, unrelated to fibrin fragments.

cards.q: What do activated protein C and protein S do?
cards.a: They inactivate factors V and VIII, slowing the cascade.
options: They cross link fibrin to stabilize the clot
They inactivate factors V and VIII, slowing the cascade
They activate factors V and VIII, speeding the cascade
They convert plasminogen to plasmin
cards.explanation: Protein C, helped by protein S, degrades two key cofactors, which keeps thrombin generation confined to the site of injury. Activating those factors is what thrombin does as part of positive feedback, the opposite role. Plasminogen activation is the job of tissue plasminogen activator. Cross linking is factor XIIIa's function.

cards.q: A patient starts warfarin today. Why does the anticoagulant effect take two to three days to appear?
cards.a: Factors already circulating remain active until they are cleared, since warfarin only affects new synthesis.
options: Warfarin acts only after existing clots have dissolved
Warfarin is stored in fat and must saturate the tissues first
Factors already in the circulation stay active until they are cleared and replaced
Warfarin must first be converted to its active form by intestinal bacteria in the gut
cards.explanation: Blocking vitamin K recycling stops the production line but does nothing to the stock already in the plasma, so clotting stays near normal until those factors are degraded over their natural half lives. Warfarin is absorbed and active without bacterial conversion. Existing clots are irrelevant to the timing, since warfarin does not act on them at all. Tissue saturation is not the reason for the delay.

cards.q: Why does heparin prevent clotting in a test tube while warfarin does not?
cards.a: Heparin acts directly on circulating antithrombin III, while warfarin acts on hepatic factor synthesis.
options: Heparin binds calcium in the sample, while warfarin binds fibrinogen
Heparin destroys platelets in the tube, while warfarin destroys red cells
Heparin is a large protein and warfarin is a simple ion, so only heparin can work outside the body
Heparin acts directly on circulating antithrombin III, while warfarin acts on liver synthesis
cards.explanation: Heparin needs only plasma components that are already in the tube, so it works immediately anywhere, while warfarin needs a functioning liver making new factors, which a test tube does not have. Calcium binding is how citrate and EDTA work, not heparin. Neither drug works by destroying cells. Heparin is a polysaccharide rather than a protein, and warfarin is a small organic molecule rather than an ion.

cards.q: A patient takes daily low dose aspirin. Predict the pattern of laboratory results.
cards.a: Bleeding time is prolonged while prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time stay normal.
options: Bleeding time is prolonged while both cascade tests stay entirely normal
Prothrombin time is prolonged while bleeding time stays normal
Both cascade tests are prolonged while the bleeding time stays entirely normal
All three tests are prolonged equally
cards.explanation: Aspirin blocks thromboxane synthesis in platelets, so the platelet phase is impaired while the plasma cascade is untouched, and only the test that measures platelet function changes. A prolonged prothrombin time with normal bleeding time is the warfarin pattern. Both cascade tests prolonged would indicate a common pathway or vitamin K problem. Nothing about aspirin affects all three tests.

cards.q: Tissue plasminogen activator is given to a patient with a fresh clot. How does its action differ from that of heparin?
cards.a: It dissolves fibrin already formed, while heparin only prevents further clot growth.
options: Neither affects existing clots; both act only on new fibrin
It dissolves fibrin already formed, while heparin only prevents further clot growth
It prevents the formation of new clots, while heparin dissolves clots already present
Both dissolve existing clots, but heparin acts faster
cards.explanation: Tissue plasminogen activator generates plasmin, which cuts fibrin apart, so it is a thrombolytic, whereas heparin accelerates antithrombin and simply stops more thrombin from acting. The roles are not reversed; heparin has no fibrin digesting ability. Heparin does not dissolve clots at any speed. Tissue plasminogen activator definitely affects existing fibrin, which is the point of giving it.

cards.q: A patient has a markedly elevated D-dimer. What does this indicate?
cards.a: A clot has formed somewhere and plasmin is breaking it down.
options: Platelet count is elevated
Vitamin K stores are depleted
A clot has formed somewhere and plasmin is breaking it down
The patient cannot form clots at all, anywhere in the circulation
cards.explanation: D-dimer is released only when cross linked fibrin is digested, so its presence proves both that clotting occurred and that fibrinolysis is under way. An inability to clot would produce no fibrin and therefore no degradation fragments. Platelet count is measured separately and is not reflected in this fragment. Vitamin K status is assessed through the prothrombin time, not through fibrin fragments.

cards.q: A patient on warfarin has excessive bleeding. What is the physiological rationale for giving vitamin K?
cards.a: Supplying vitamin K restores the liver's ability to make functional factors II, VII, IX, and X.
options: Vitamin K binds warfarin in the plasma and inactivates it
Vitamin K directly cross links the fibrin strands at each bleeding site in the body
Vitamin K stimulates the marrow to make more platelets
Supplying vitamin K lets the liver make functional factors II, VII, IX, and X again
cards.explanation: Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, so flooding the system with the vitamin lets the liver resume adding calcium binding sites to those four factors, though the effect takes hours because new protein must be synthesized. Vitamin K does not chemically neutralize warfarin in the plasma. Cross linking fibrin is factor XIIIa's job and requires no vitamin K. Platelet production is driven by thrombopoietin, not by vitamin K.

cards.q: A patient stabilized on warfarin greatly increases their intake of leafy green vegetables, which are rich in vitamin K. Predict the effect on clotting.
cards.a: Clotting speeds up, because more vitamin K competes with the drug and more functional factors are made.
options: Clotting speeds up, because more vitamin K competes with the drug at the same enzyme
Clotting slows further, because vitamin K adds to the anticoagulant effect
Clotting is unchanged, because dietary vitamin K is not absorbed
Clotting speeds up, because the extra vitamin K directly activates thrombin in the plasma
cards.explanation: Warfarin and vitamin K work against each other at the same enzyme, so raising vitamin K supply partly overcomes the block and the liver produces more working factors, shortening clotting times. Vitamin K opposes warfarin rather than adding to it. Dietary vitamin K is absorbed with fats and does reach the liver. The vitamin acts during hepatic synthesis, not by activating thrombin already in the plasma.

cards.q: A hospitalized patient is receiving both heparin and aspirin. Which laboratory findings would you expect?
cards.a: A prolonged partial thromboplastin time from the heparin and a prolonged bleeding time from the aspirin.
options: A prolonged bleeding time from the heparin and a prolonged prothrombin time from the aspirin
A prolonged partial thromboplastin time from the heparin and a prolonged bleeding time from the aspirin
A prolonged prothrombin time from the heparin and a normal bleeding time despite the aspirin
A normal partial thromboplastin time, since heparin acts only on platelets
cards.explanation: The two drugs act on different arms of hemostasis, so each shows up in the test that examines its arm: heparin boosts antithrombin and slows the intrinsic and common pathways, while aspirin blocks thromboxane and slows platelet plug formation. Heparin's main effect is on the partial thromboplastin time rather than the prothrombin time. Heparin acts on plasma proteases, not on platelets, so it certainly changes a cascade test. The last option assigns each drug the other's effect.

cards.q: A patient with a deep vein clot is given tissue plasminogen activator. Trace what happens in the clot.
cards.a: Plasminogen trapped in the clot becomes plasmin, plasmin digests fibrin, and fragments including D-dimer appear in the blood.
options: Factor XIII is activated, fibrin is cross linked further, and the clot hardens
Vitamin K is blocked, the new factors are nonfunctional, and the existing clot slowly shrinks away
Plasminogen in the clot becomes plasmin, plasmin digests fibrin, and D-dimer appears in the blood
Thrombin is inactivated, fibrinogen levels rise, and no fragments are released
cards.explanation: The drug activates the enzyme system already built into the clot, and the debris from cross linked fibrin is what the D-dimer test detects, so the sequence has a measurable endpoint. Inactivating thrombin describes heparin's action and would not release fibrin fragments. Activating factor XIII would strengthen the clot rather than remove it. Blocking vitamin K describes warfarin and does not dismantle fibrin that already exists.

cards.q: A patient has an inherited deficiency of antithrombin III. Predict the clotting tendency and the response to heparin.
cards.a: An increased tendency to form clots, and a reduced response to heparin because heparin works through antithrombin III.
options: An increased tendency to bleed, and an exaggerated response to heparin
An increased tendency to form clots, and a greatly exaggerated response to heparin treatment
No change in clotting, but a reduced response to warfarin
An increased tendency to form clots, and a reduced response to heparin
cards.explanation: Antithrombin III is the main brake on thrombin, so having too little leaves clotting unchecked, and because heparin acts by accelerating that same brake, the drug has little to accelerate. The tendency is toward clotting rather than bleeding, since the missing protein is an anticoagulant. The response to heparin is reduced rather than exaggerated, for the same mechanistic reason. Clotting is definitely changed, and warfarin acts through vitamin K rather than through antithrombin III.

cards.q: A person with type A blood has which antigen on their erythrocytes and which antibody in their plasma?
cards.a: A antigen on the cells and anti-B antibody in the plasma.
options: A antigen on the cells and anti-B antibody in the plasma
A antigen on the cells and anti-A antibody in the plasma
B antigen on the cells and anti-A antibody in the plasma
No antigen on the cells and anti-B antibody in the plasma
cards.explanation: The rule is that you carry antibodies against the ABO antigen you lack, so a type A person makes anti-B and tolerates A. Having anti-A along with A antigen would mean attacking your own cells, which does not happen in a healthy person. B antigen with anti-A describes type B, not type A. No antigen with anti-B alone matches no ABO type, since a person lacking both antigens has both antibodies.

cards.q: A person with type B blood has which antigen and which antibody?
cards.a: B antigen on the cells and anti-A antibody in the plasma.
options: B antigen on the cells and no ABO antibody
B antigen on the cells and anti-A antibody in the plasma
B antigen on the cells and anti-B antibody in the plasma
A antigen on the cells and anti-B antibody in the plasma
cards.explanation: You make antibodies against the antigen you do not have, so type B carries anti-A. Carrying anti-B with B antigen would mean self attack and does not occur. A antigen with anti-B is the type A pattern. Having no ABO antibody at all is the type AB pattern, which requires both antigens to be present.

cards.q: A person with type AB blood has which antigens and which antibodies?
cards.a: Both A and B antigens, and neither anti-A nor anti-B.
options: Neither A nor B antigen, and neither anti-A nor anti-B
Neither A nor B antigen, and both anti-A and anti-B
Both A and B antigens, and neither anti-A nor anti-B
Both A and B antigens, and both anti-A and anti-B
cards.explanation: Because a type AB person carries both antigens, they can make antibodies against neither, which is why AB is the universal recipient for ABO purposes. Having both antibodies alongside both antigens would destroy their own cells. Having neither antigen is the type O pattern, not AB. Neither antigen with both antibodies is exactly type O, the opposite of AB.

cards.q: A person with type O blood has which antigens and which antibodies?
cards.a: Neither A nor B antigen, and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
options: Neither A nor B antigen, and neither anti-A nor anti-B
Both A and B antigens, and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
Both A and B antigens, and neither anti-A nor anti-B
Neither A nor B antigen, and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
cards.explanation: Type O cells carry no A or B antigen, so the plasma is free to contain antibodies against both, which makes type O red cells safe to give but type O plasma the most reactive. Having no antigen and no antibody is not a natural ABO type. Both antigens with both antibodies would mean self destruction. Both antigens with no antibody is type AB, the mirror image of type O.

cards.q: Which blood type is the universal red cell donor?
cards.a: Type O negative.
options: Type O negative
Type AB positive
Type A negative
Type O positive
cards.explanation: O negative cells display neither A nor B antigen nor the D antigen, so there is nothing on their surface for a recipient's antibodies to attack. AB positive is the universal recipient, not the universal donor, because its cells carry every common antigen. A negative cells still carry the A antigen and would be attacked by anti-A. O positive cells are safe for ABO but carry D and can sensitize an Rh negative recipient.

cards.q: Which blood type is the universal recipient of red cells?
cards.a: Type AB positive.
options: Type O positive
Type AB positive
Type O negative
Type AB negative
cards.explanation: An AB positive person makes neither anti-A nor anti-B and already has the D antigen, so no common donor red cell carries an antigen their plasma will attack. O negative is the universal donor, the opposite role. AB negative lacks D, so it can still react to Rh positive cells if the person has been sensitized. O positive plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B, making it a poor recipient of A, B, or AB cells.

cards.q: The naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B antibodies are mostly which immunoglobulin class, and what does that mean for the placenta?
cards.a: IgM, which is too large to cross the placenta.
options: IgE, which crosses the placenta readily
IgA, which is secreted into the amniotic fluid
IgM, which is too large to cross the placenta
IgG, which crosses the placenta readily
cards.explanation: ABO antibodies arise without deliberate immunization and are predominantly pentameric IgM, so they stay in the maternal circulation and rarely cause severe fetal disease. IgG is the class that does cross, and anti-D is IgG, which is precisely why Rh incompatibility is the classic cause of hemolytic disease of the newborn. IgE mediates allergy and does not cross the placenta. IgA is the secretory antibody of mucosal surfaces and is not the ABO antibody class.

cards.q: When does an Rh negative person develop anti-D antibodies?
cards.a: Only after exposure to Rh positive red cells.
options: From birth, in the same way as anti-A and anti-B
Whenever plasma D antigen concentration falls
Only if they also lack both A and B antigens
Only after exposure to Rh positive red cells
cards.explanation: Anti-D is not naturally occurring; the immune system must first meet the D antigen through transfusion or through fetal cells entering the maternal circulation, and only then does it produce antibody. ABO antibodies are present from infancy without deliberate exposure, which is the key difference between the two systems. There is no plasma D antigen level to sense. ABO type has no bearing on whether a person can become sensitized to D.

cards.q: Type A red cells are transfused into a type B recipient. What happens and why?
cards.a: Agglutination, because the recipient's anti-A antibodies bind the donor A antigens.
options: Agglutination, because the recipient's anti-A antibodies bind the donor A antigens
No reaction, because the donor cells carry no antigen the recipient can attack
Agglutination, because the donor's anti-B antibodies attack the recipient's cells
No reaction, because A and B antigens are compatible with each other
cards.explanation: A type B recipient carries anti-A, and the incoming cells display A, so the antibodies bridge the donor cells into clumps and hemolysis follows. There certainly is an antigen present, namely A, so the second option misstates the donor cells. The donor's own antibodies are diluted in the recipient's much larger plasma volume and are not the main problem, so the reaction is driven by recipient antibody against donor antigen. A and B are not compatible; each is the target of the other's antibody.

cards.q: Type O red cells are transfused into a type A recipient. What happens and why?
cards.a: No agglutination, because the donor cells carry neither A nor B antigen.
options: No agglutination, because type A recipients have no antibodies
No agglutination, because the donor cells carry neither A nor B antigen
Agglutination, because the recipient's anti-B attacks the donor cells
Agglutination, because type O cells carry both A and B antigens
cards.explanation: The recipient's anti-B has nothing to bind on a type O cell, since those cells display no A or B antigen, which is what makes O the universal red cell donor. Anti-B is present in the type A recipient, but it needs a B antigen to attack and there is none. Type O cells lack both antigens rather than carrying both. Type A recipients do have an antibody, anti-B, so the last option is wrong about the mechanism even though the outcome is right.

cards.q: Why can a type AB recipient safely receive red cells of any ABO type?
cards.a: Their plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B, so no ABO antibody is available to attack donor cells.
options: Their plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B, which neutralize each other before they can act on donor cells
Their red cells carry the D antigen, which suppresses ABO reactions
Their plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B, so no antibody can attack the donor cells
Their red cells carry no antigens, so nothing can be recognized
cards.explanation: Compatibility in a red cell transfusion is decided by what antibodies the recipient has, and an AB person has no ABO antibodies at all, so any donor red cell passes unchallenged. Their cells carry both antigens rather than none; it is the antibody side that makes them universal recipients. They do not have both antibodies, and antibodies against different antigens would not neutralize each other anyway. The D antigen belongs to a separate system and does not suppress ABO reactions.

cards.q: An Rh negative person with no prior exposure receives Rh positive red cells for the first time. What is the immediate result?
cards.a: Usually no immediate reaction, but the person becomes sensitized and makes anti-D over the following weeks.
options: Immediate severe agglutination, because anti-D is present from birth
No reaction and no sensitization, because D is not immunogenic
Immediate agglutination, because the donor plasma anti-D attacks the recipient's own cells
Usually no immediate reaction, but the person becomes sensitized and makes anti-D later
cards.explanation: Anti-D is not naturally present, so the first exposure has nothing to react with, but it primes the immune system and antibody appears afterward, setting up trouble on a later exposure. Anti-D is not present from birth, which is the central difference from the ABO antibodies. The D antigen is strongly immunogenic, so sensitization does occur. An Rh positive donor has no anti-D to give, since a person does not make antibody against their own antigen.

cards.q: A previously sensitized Rh negative patient receives Rh positive red cells. Predict the outcome.
cards.a: The existing anti-D binds the donor cells and causes agglutination and hemolysis.
options: The existing anti-D binds the donor cells and causes agglutination and hemolysis
No reaction, because sensitization only affects pregnancy
No reaction, because anti-D disappears from the plasma within a few days of forming
The donor cells lose the D antigen and are tolerated
cards.explanation: Once anti-D exists, any D positive cell entering the circulation is a target, so the second exposure produces the reaction that the first one did not. Sensitization is not limited to pregnancy; a transfusion can sensitize a person just as fetal cells can. Antibody and memory cells persist for years, so the response does not fade in days. Red cells do not shed their antigens to escape recognition.

cards.q: A patient's plasma agglutinates both type A and type B test cells. What is the patient's ABO type?
cards.a: Type O.
options: Type B
Type O
Type AB
Type A
cards.explanation: Agglutinating both means the plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B, and only a type O person carries both, because they carry neither antigen. Type AB plasma has no ABO antibody and would agglutinate neither. Type A plasma has only anti-B and would agglutinate B cells alone. Type B plasma has only anti-A and would agglutinate A cells alone.

cards.q: Type B red cells are transfused into a type AB recipient. Predict the outcome.
cards.a: No agglutination, because the recipient has no anti-B to attack the donor B antigen.
options: Agglutination, because the donor's anti-A binds the recipient's A antigen
No agglutination, because the donor cells carry no antigen at all
No agglutination, because the recipient has no anti-B to attack the donor B antigen
Agglutination, because the recipient's anti-B binds the donor B antigen
cards.explanation: An AB recipient makes neither ABO antibody, so donor B cells are not recognized and the transfusion is compatible. The recipient does not have anti-B, since they carry the B antigen themselves. The donor plasma anti-A is present in only a small volume in a red cell unit and is not the deciding factor in red cell compatibility. Type B cells do carry an antigen, namely B, so the last option misstates the donor.

cards.q: An Rh negative woman carries an Rh positive fetus. Why is the first such pregnancy usually unaffected while a later one is at risk?
cards.a: Fetal cells usually enter the maternal circulation at delivery, so anti-D is made after the first birth and crosses the placenta in the next pregnancy.
options: Anti-D is present from birth in every Rh negative woman, so the very first Rh positive fetus is attacked most severely
The first fetus is protected because IgM antibodies cross the placenta easily and dilute the response
The second fetus is at risk only if it is Rh negative, since D antigen accumulates over pregnancies
Fetal cells usually enter the maternal circulation at delivery, so anti-D is made only after the first birth
cards.explanation: The timing is everything: the mother is exposed near the end of the first pregnancy, so her anti-D appears after that fetus is already delivered, and it is the IgG anti-D crossing the placenta in a later Rh positive pregnancy that destroys fetal red cells. Anti-D is never naturally present before exposure, which is why the first pregnancy is generally safe. IgM does not cross the placenta at all, and it would not be protective if it did. Only an Rh positive fetus carries the D antigen, so an Rh negative fetus is not a target.

cards.q: An Rh negative pregnant woman is given anti-D immune globulin at 28 weeks and again after delivery. How does this prevent hemolytic disease of the newborn?
cards.a: The injected antibody clears fetal Rh positive cells before the mother's own immune system is sensitized to D.
options: The injected antibody clears fetal Rh positive cells before the mother is sensitized
It converts the fetus from Rh positive to Rh negative
It blocks the placenta so no maternal antibody can cross
It destroys the mother's existing anti-D antibodies left over from her earlier pregnancies
cards.explanation: Passive antibody removes the fetal cells from the maternal circulation quickly, so her B lymphocytes never mount a primary response and no memory is established for the next pregnancy. Nothing can change the fetal genotype, so conversion is impossible. The placenta is not blocked; IgG transfer continues normally for all other antibodies. The treatment prevents sensitization rather than reversing it, which is why it is useless once a woman has already made her own anti-D.

cards.q: A trauma patient arrives unconscious with unknown blood type and needs red cells immediately. Why is O negative the safest choice?
cards.a: O negative cells lack A, B, and D antigens, so no antibody the recipient could have will find a target.
options: O negative cells are the only ones that carry the D antigen, which suppresses agglutination
O negative cells lack A, B, and D antigens, so no antibody the recipient could have will find a target
O negative plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B, which protect the recipient's own cells
O negative cells carry all three antigens, so they match any recipient
cards.explanation: Compatibility depends on whether the recipient's antibodies can bind something on the donor cell, and an O negative cell presents none of the three common antigens, so the reaction cannot start. O negative plasma does contain both antibodies, but that is a hazard rather than a protection, which is why red cells are given with most of the plasma removed. O negative cells lack antigens rather than carrying all of them. O negative means D is absent, so the last option contradicts itself.

cards.q: A patient types as A negative. Which donor red cell units are safe, and why?
cards.a: A negative and O negative, because the patient has anti-B and could be sensitized to D.
options: AB negative and B negative, because those units lack the A antigen the patient already has
Any negative unit, because Rh negative blood is compatible with every ABO type
A negative and O negative, because the patient has anti-B and could be sensitized to D
A positive and O positive, because the D antigen is harmless in ABO matched blood
cards.explanation: Two rules run at once: the recipient's anti-B rules out any unit carrying B, and the absence of D means Rh positive cells could sensitize the patient, so only A negative and O negative units satisfy both. Rh positive units are not harmless to an Rh negative recipient, since D is strongly immunogenic. AB negative and B negative units both carry the B antigen that the patient's anti-B will attack. Being Rh negative does not make a unit ABO compatible; a B negative unit still has B antigen.

cards.q: In what units is hematocrit reported?
cards.a: As a percentage of total blood volume.
options: In grams per deciliter
In cells per microliter
In millimeters of packed column
As a percentage of total blood volume
cards.explanation: Hematocrit is a ratio of the packed red cell column to the whole column, so it is expressed as a percent and has no mass or count units. Grams per deciliter is the unit for hemoglobin concentration. Cells per microliter is the unit for a red cell count. Column length in millimeters is what you measure, but you must divide it by the total length to get the reported value.

cards.q: What does the microhematocrit centrifuge do to a blood sample?
cards.a: It separates the components by density, packing red cells at the bottom of the tube.
options: It separates the components by density, packing red cells at the bottom of the tube
It lyses the red cells so that the hemoglobin they contain can be measured directly in the plasma
It removes the anticoagulant so the sample can clot
It warms the sample so plasma proteins dissolve
cards.explanation: High speed spinning drives the densest elements, the red cells, to the closed end, with the buffy coat above them and plasma on top, and the relative lengths of those layers give the hematocrit. Lysing cells is what a hemoglobin assay does chemically, not what the centrifuge does. The anticoagulant remains in the sample throughout. Warming is not part of the procedure and plasma proteins are already dissolved.

cards.q: Why is the capillary tube used for a microhematocrit coated with heparin?
cards.a: To prevent the sample from clotting before it can be spun.
options: To bind hemoglobin so it can be measured on the same tube
To prevent the sample from clotting before it can be spun
To lyse the white cells so the buffy coat disappears
To make the red cells denser so they pack faster
cards.explanation: A clotted sample cannot be separated into layers, so the tube carries an anticoagulant that keeps the cells suspended until centrifugation. Heparin does not lyse white cells, and the buffy coat should still be visible. It does not change red cell density. Hemoglobin is measured by a separate method on a separate portion of sample.

cards.q: Why is one end of the filled capillary tube sealed with clay before spinning?
cards.a: To keep the sample from being thrown out of the tube during centrifugation.
options: To mark which end contains the plasma
To absorb the plasma so only cells remain
To keep the sample from being thrown out of the tube during centrifugation
To provide the calcium that the red cells need in order to pack down tightly
cards.explanation: Spinning generates a large outward force, and an unsealed tube would lose sample, giving an inaccurate and messy result. The clay is inert and supplies no reagent to the reaction.
