Layer identification comes from the visible color boundaries, not from the seal. Nothing is absorbed by the clay; the plasma remains in the tube above the cells.

cards.q: In a spun microhematocrit tube, where is the buffy coat and what should you do with it when reading the result?
cards.a: It lies between the packed red cells and the plasma, and it is excluded from the red cell column.
options: It lies at the sealed end below the red cells, and it is included in the red cell column
It lies at the top of the plasma, and it is included in the total column
It is dissolved in the plasma and cannot be seen
It lies between the packed red cells and the plasma, and it is excluded from the red cell column
cards.explanation: White cells and platelets are less dense than red cells but denser than plasma, so they form a thin pale band at the interface that is not part of the red cell measurement. Nothing packs below the red cells, which are the densest component. The buffy coat is not at the top, and the total column does include it as part of whole blood. It is visible as a distinct layer, usually about 1 percent of the column.

cards.q: What is the normal hemoglobin range for an adult male?
cards.a: About 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL.
options: About 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL
About 42 to 52 g/dL
About 4.5 to 6.0 g/dL
About 30 to 40 g/dL
cards.explanation: Hemoglobin concentration in men runs in the mid teens in grams per deciliter, roughly one third of the hematocrit value. The 42 to 52 range is the male hematocrit in percent, not a hemoglobin in g/dL. A value of 4.5 to 6.0 g/dL would be a life threatening anemia. A value of 30 to 40 g/dL is far above anything physiologically possible.

cards.q: What is the normal hemoglobin range for an adult female?
cards.a: About 12.0 to 16.0 g/dL.
options: About 20 to 25 g/dL
About 12.0 to 16.0 g/dL
About 37 to 47 g/dL
About 6.0 to 8.0 g/dL
cards.explanation: Women run slightly lower than men, with a lower limit around 12 g/dL, below which anemia is diagnosed. The 37 to 47 range is the female hematocrit in percent. A value of 6.0 to 8.0 g/dL would be a severe anemia. A value of 20 to 25 g/dL is above any normal human value and would suggest an error.

cards.q: What is the rule of three that links hemoglobin and hematocrit?
cards.a: Hematocrit is approximately three times the hemoglobin in g/dL.
options: Hematocrit plus hemoglobin equals 60 in a healthy adult
Hemoglobin equals hematocrit divided by ten
Hematocrit is approximately three times the hemoglobin in g/dL
Hemoglobin is approximately three times the hematocrit
cards.explanation: A hemoglobin of 15 g/dL corresponds to a hematocrit near 45 percent, so multiplying by three gives a quick internal check on whether two results agree. Reversing the relationship would predict a hemoglobin of 135 from a hematocrit of 45, which is impossible. Adding the two values has no physiological meaning. Dividing by ten would predict a hemoglobin of 4.5 from a hematocrit of 45, far below the normal range.

cards.q: A student measures the packed red cell column as 21 mm and the total column of blood as 50 mm. What is the hematocrit?
cards.a: 42 percent.
options: 21 percent
50 percent
71 percent
42 percent
cards.explanation: Divide the red cell column by the total column and multiply by 100, so 21 divided by 50 is 0.42, or 42 percent, a normal adult value. Reporting 21 mistakes the raw length for the ratio. Reporting 50 gives the total column length rather than the fraction. Adding the two numbers gives 71 and has no meaning as a ratio.

cards.q: A student includes the buffy coat in the packed red cell column when reading the tube. What is the effect on the reported hematocrit?
cards.a: It is slightly falsely high.
options: It is slightly falsely high
It is slightly falsely low
It is unaffected
It is falsely high by about half
cards.explanation: Adding the white cell and platelet layer lengthens the numerator without changing the denominator, so the percentage comes out a point or so above the true value. It cannot be falsely low, since nothing was subtracted. It is not unaffected, because the numerator changed. The buffy coat is only about 1 percent of the column, so the error is small rather than enormous.

cards.q: A capillary tube is inadequately sealed and some blood escapes during centrifugation, with cells lost preferentially from the packed end. What happens to the reported hematocrit?
cards.a: It reads falsely low, because the red cell column is shortened.
options: It cannot be read at all, because the layers will not separate
It reads falsely low, because the red cell column is shortened
It reads falsely high, because plasma is lost first
It is unaffected, because the ratio is preserved
cards.explanation: Losing packed cells from the sealed end reduces the numerator relative to the total, so the calculated percentage falls below the true value. Plasma is not the fraction lost at the sealed end, so the error does not go upward for that reason. The ratio is not preserved when one component is selectively lost. Separation still occurs; it is the measurement that is wrong.

cards.q: A sample is spun for too short a time, leaving plasma trapped among the packed red cells. What happens to the reported hematocrit?
cards.a: It reads falsely high, because the red cell column includes trapped plasma.
options: It is unaffected, because trapped plasma is part of blood anyway
It reads falsely low, because the buffy coat expands
It reads falsely high, because the red cell column includes trapped plasma
It reads falsely low, because some cells stay suspended in the plasma
cards.explanation: Incomplete packing leaves fluid between the cells, so the column measured as red cells is longer than the true cell volume and the percentage is overstated. Cells left suspended would also be a problem, but under spinning primarily leaves plasma trapped in a loosely packed column, pushing the value up. Trapped plasma is part of blood but it is not part of the red cell fraction being measured. The buffy coat does not expand with shorter spinning in a way that would lower the reading.

cards.q: A patient's hemoglobin is 10 g/dL. Using the rule of three, what hematocrit would you expect, and how would you interpret it?
cards.a: About 30 percent, which is below the normal range for either sex and indicates anemia.
options: About 30 percent, which sits comfortably within the normal reference range for an adult female
About 3 percent, which is incompatible with life
About 45 percent, which is normal for either sex
About 30 percent, which is below the normal range for either sex and indicates anemia
cards.explanation: Multiplying 10 by three predicts a hematocrit near 30 percent, well under the female range of 37 to 47 and the male range of 42 to 52, so the patient is anemic. Thirty percent is not within the female range, which starts at about 37. Three percent would come from dividing rather than multiplying and is not compatible with life. Forty five percent would correspond to a hemoglobin of about 15 g/dL, not 10.

cards.q: An adult female's hematocrit measures 49 percent on a properly performed test. How should this be interpreted?
cards.a: Above the female reference range, which should prompt a look at hydration status and other causes.
options: Above the female reference range, which should prompt a look at hydration status
Within the female reference range and entirely expected
Below the female reference range, indicating anemia
Impossible, since the hematocrit of any healthy adult cannot exceed 47 percent by definition
cards.explanation: The female range tops out near 47 percent, so 49 is high and the common explanations are hemoconcentration from fluid loss or a true increase in red cell mass. It is not within the range, and calling it expected would miss a real finding. It is well above rather than below any anemia threshold. Hematocrit can certainly exceed 47 percent, reaching 60 or more in polycythemia.

cards.q: A blood sample is drawn from a severely dehydrated patient. How does this affect the hematocrit as a measure of red cell mass?
cards.a: The hematocrit overstates red cell mass, because plasma volume is reduced.
options: The hematocrit cannot be measured until fluids are given
The hematocrit overstates red cell mass, because plasma volume is reduced
The hematocrit understates red cell mass, because cells shrink when dehydrated
The hematocrit measures red cell mass accurately regardless of hydration
cards.explanation: Hematocrit is a ratio, so shrinking the plasma denominator raises the percentage even though the number of red cells has not changed, which is why a dehydrated patient can look falsely normal or falsely polycythemic. Red cells do not shrink appreciably with whole body dehydration, since plasma osmolarity changes only modestly. Hydration status matters greatly, so the measurement is not independent of it. The test can be performed at any time; the difficulty is in interpreting it.

cards.q: A student reports a hematocrit of 62 percent and a hemoglobin of 14 g/dL on the same sample. What should be concluded?
cards.a: The two results are inconsistent by the rule of three, so at least one measurement is in error.
options: The results are consistent and indicate anemia
The results are consistent, because hemoglobin and hematocrit are unrelated measurements
The two results are inconsistent by the rule of three, so one measurement is in error
The results are consistent and indicate polycythemia
cards.explanation: A hemoglobin of 14 predicts a hematocrit near 42, so a reading of 62 is far outside the expected relationship and points to a technique problem such as under spinning or a misread column. True polycythemia would raise both values together, giving a hemoglobin near 20. Anemia would lower both. The two measurements are closely related because both reflect red cell content, which is exactly what makes the internal check useful.

cards.q: A 20 year old female runner has a hematocrit of 33 percent and a hemoglobin of 11 g/dL. Evaluate these results together.
cards.a: They are internally consistent and both fall below the female reference range, indicating anemia.
options: They are internally inconsistent, so the sample must be repeated before any interpretation
They are consistent and both fall within the female reference range
They are consistent and indicate polycythemia from endurance training
They are internally consistent and both fall below the female reference range, indicating anemia
cards.explanation: Eleven times three is 33, so the pair passes the rule of three check, and both numbers sit under the female ranges of 12 to 16 g/dL and 37 to 47 percent, so the finding is a real anemia rather than a laboratory artifact. There is no inconsistency to force a repeat on technical grounds. Neither value is within the reference range. Polycythemia would mean values above the range, the opposite of what is shown.

cards.q: A dehydrated patient has a hematocrit of 54 percent on admission and 44 percent after 2 L of intravenous fluid. Which value better reflects red cell mass, and why?
cards.a: The post fluid value, because restoring plasma volume removes the hemoconcentration that inflated the first result.
options: The post fluid value, because restoring plasma volume removes the hemoconcentration
The admission value, because it was measured before any dilution by treatment
Neither, because intravenous fluid destroys red cells and invalidates both
Both equally, since the number of red cells did not change at all between the two draws
cards.explanation: The red cell count was the same for both draws, so the difference is entirely in the denominator, and the value obtained at a normal plasma volume is the one that represents red cell mass fairly. The admission value was measured on an abnormally small plasma volume, so being first does not make it more valid. Isotonic fluid does not destroy red cells. The cell number being constant is precisely why the two percentages cannot both be right about red cell mass.

cards.q: A sample leaks during centrifugation, losing packed red cells, and hemoglobin is measured on a separate uncompromised sample. Predict the pattern of results.
cards.a: A falsely low hematocrit with a normal hemoglobin, so the rule of three check fails.
options: Both values normal, since a leak affects only the appearance of the tube
A falsely low hematocrit with a normal hemoglobin, so the rule of three check fails
A falsely high hematocrit with a normal hemoglobin, so the rule of three check fails
Both values falsely low, so the rule of three check still passes
cards.explanation: Only the spun tube was compromised, so the shortened red cell column drives the percentage down while the separately measured hemoglobin is unaffected, and the mismatch flags the error. Losing cells cannot raise the hematocrit. The hemoglobin sample was intact, so both values are not affected. The leak changes the measurement, not just the appearance, which is why the discrepancy appears.

cards.q: Which three antisera are used in a standard ABO and Rh typing slide?
cards.a: Anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D.
options: Anti-AB, anti-O, and anti-D
Anti-A, anti-B, and anti-fibrinogen
Anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D
Anti-A, anti-O, and anti-Rh negative
cards.explanation: Each reagent contains antibody against one antigen, so three wells test for the A antigen, the B antigen, and the D antigen of the Rh system. There is no O antigen and therefore no anti-O reagent; type O is identified by the absence of reactions. Rh negative means the absence of D, so no reagent can test for it directly. Fibrinogen is a clotting protein and has nothing to do with blood group antigens.

cards.q: What does agglutination in a typing well indicate?
cards.a: The antibody in that antiserum has bound its matching antigen on the red cells, clumping them.
options: The red cells have lysed and released hemoglobin
The sample has clotted because it was collected without any anticoagulant present
The antigen being tested for is absent
The antibody in that antiserum has bound its matching antigen on the red cells
cards.explanation: Each antibody has multiple binding sites, so it bridges neighboring cells into visible clumps, and clumping is therefore a positive result for that antigen. Hemolysis is a separate event that may follow in the body but is not what you read on the slide. Clotting is a fibrin reaction involving plasma proteins and looks different from agglutination. Absence of the antigen produces a smooth, evenly red suspension with no clumping.

cards.q: A sample agglutinates with anti-A but not with anti-B. What ABO type is it?
cards.a: Type A.
options: Type A
Type B
Type AB
Type O
cards.explanation: Clumping with anti-A means the A antigen is present, and no clumping with anti-B means the B antigen is absent, which is the definition of type A. Type B would clump with anti-B instead. Type AB would clump with both reagents. Type O would clump with neither.

cards.q: A sample agglutinates with both anti-A and anti-B. What ABO type is it?
cards.a: Type AB.
options: Type B
Type AB
Type O
Type A
cards.explanation: Reacting with both reagents means both the A and the B antigen are on the cells, which is type AB. Type O carries neither antigen and clumps with neither reagent. Type A clumps only with anti-A. Type B clumps only with anti-B.

cards.q: A sample shows no agglutination with anti-A, anti-B, or anti-D. What is the full type?
cards.a: O negative.
options: O positive
AB negative
O negative
AB positive
cards.explanation: No reaction anywhere means none of the three antigens is present, so the cells are type O and Rh negative, the universal red cell donor. AB positive would clump in all three wells. O positive would clump with anti-D only. AB negative would clump with anti-A and anti-B but not anti-D.

cards.q: What antigen does the anti-D reagent detect?
cards.a: The D antigen, which determines Rh positive status.
options: The A antigen on type A cells
The fibrin present in a clotted sample
The antibody present in the patient's plasma
The D antigen, which determines Rh positive status
cards.explanation: The D antigen is the clinically important member of the Rh system, so its presence is what the label Rh positive reports. The A antigen is detected by the anti-A reagent in a different well. Fibrin is not a blood group antigen and would not be part of a typing panel. Forward typing examines antigens on the patient's red cells, not antibodies in their plasma.

cards.q: In forward typing on a slide, what is being tested?
cards.a: The antigens present on the patient's red cells.
options: The antigens present on the patient's red cells
The antibodies present in the patient's plasma
The hemoglobin concentration of the sample
The number of platelets in the sample
cards.explanation: Forward typing mixes the patient's cells with known antibodies, so the result tells you which surface antigens are there. Testing the patient's plasma against known cells is reverse typing, the confirmatory step that runs in the opposite direction. Hemoglobin concentration requires a separate assay. Platelet counts are unrelated to blood group determination.

cards.q: What does a typing antiserum contain?
cards.a: Antibodies directed against one specific red cell antigen.
options: Anticoagulant that prevents clumping
Antibodies directed against one specific red cell antigen
Red cells collected from a donor whose ABO blood type is known
Purified antigen from a donor
cards.explanation: Anti-A serum contains anti-A antibody, and so on, so mixing it with unknown cells reveals whether that antigen is present. Known red cells are the reagent used in reverse typing, the mirror image of this test. Purified antigen would not clump cells, since clumping requires the bridging action of antibody. An anticoagulant prevents fibrin formation and would defeat the purpose of a test that depends on visible clumping.

cards.q: A sample agglutinates with anti-B and anti-D but not with anti-A. What is the full type?
cards.a: B positive.
options: B negative
AB positive
B positive
A positive
cards.explanation: Clumping with anti-B places the B antigen on the cells, no clumping with anti-A rules out A, and clumping with anti-D makes it Rh positive. A positive would have required a reaction with anti-A instead. B negative would have shown no reaction in the anti-D well. AB positive would have clumped with anti-A as well.

cards.q: A sample agglutinates with anti-A and anti-D but not with anti-B. Which donor red cell types are compatible for this patient?
cards.a: A positive, A negative, O positive, and O negative.
options: A positive, B positive, AB positive, and O positive
A negative and O negative only
Only A positive, since the type must match exactly
A positive, A negative, O positive, and O negative
cards.explanation: The patient is A positive, so their plasma has anti-B and any unit carrying B is excluded, while their own D antigen means Rh positive units are also acceptable. Including B positive and AB positive units would supply the B antigen that anti-B will attack. Restricting to Rh negative units alone is safe but unnecessarily narrow for a patient who already has the D antigen. Requiring an exact match ignores the fact that O cells carry no A or B antigen and are therefore compatible.

cards.q: A sample shows no reaction with anti-A or anti-B but agglutinates with anti-D. What is the full type, and what does the plasma contain?
cards.a: O positive, with both anti-A and anti-B in the plasma.
options: O positive, with both anti-A and anti-B in the plasma
O negative, with both anti-A and anti-B in the plasma
AB positive, with neither anti-A nor anti-B in the plasma
O positive, with anti-D in the plasma
cards.explanation: No ABO antigens plus the D antigen makes this O positive, and because the person lacks both A and B they carry antibodies against both. O negative would have shown no reaction with anti-D, which contradicts the result. AB positive would have clumped with both ABO reagents. An Rh positive person does not make anti-D, since D is their own antigen.

cards.q: A patient types as AB negative. Which donor red cell types are compatible?
cards.a: AB negative, A negative, B negative, and O negative.
options: Every type, since AB is the universal recipient
AB negative, A negative, B negative, and O negative
AB positive, A positive, B positive, and O positive
AB negative and O negative only
cards.explanation: Having no ABO antibodies opens every ABO type, but lacking the D antigen means only Rh negative units avoid the risk of sensitizing the patient to D. The positive units all carry D and are therefore not the safe choice for an Rh negative recipient. Limiting to AB negative and O negative leaves out A negative and B negative units that would not be attacked, since the patient has no ABO antibodies. The universal recipient label applies fully only to AB positive.

cards.q: A student's sample agglutinates in all three wells. What is the type and what does it mean for donating?
cards.a: AB positive, which can receive from anyone but can donate red cells only to other AB positive recipients.
options: AB positive, which can donate to anyone because it carries all antigens
AB negative, since agglutination with anti-D indicates the absence of D
AB positive, which can receive from anyone but can donate only to AB positive recipients
O negative, which can donate red cells to anyone but can receive only from other O negative donors
cards.explanation: Carrying A, B and D means no recipient antibody can be present that would attack these cells in an AB positive person, but every other recipient has at least one antibody that would, so the donation range is narrow. O negative would have shown no reaction at all. Carrying all the antigens makes a poor donor, not a universal one; it is the absence of antigens that makes a universal donor. Agglutination with anti-D means D is present, so the last option reverses the reading.

cards.q: In reverse typing, a patient's plasma is mixed with known type A cells and agglutination occurs. What does this tell you?
cards.a: The plasma contains anti-A, so the patient is type B or type O.
options: The plasma contains anti-B, so the patient is type A or type O
The patient's cells carry the A antigen, so the patient is type A or AB
The patient has no ABO antibodies, so the patient is type AB
The plasma contains anti-A, so the patient is type B or type O
cards.explanation: Clumping known A cells means the plasma holds anti-A, and only people who lack the A antigen carry that antibody, which narrows the type to B or O. Anti-B would be revealed by testing against known B cells, a different well. Reverse typing examines plasma antibodies, not the patient's own cell antigens. A patient with no ABO antibodies would produce no clumping in any reverse typing well.

cards.q: Which blood type can donate red cells to the largest number of recipients, and why?
cards.a: O negative, because its cells display neither A, nor B, nor D antigen.
options: O negative, because its cells display neither A, nor B, nor D antigen
AB positive, because its plasma contains no ABO antibodies
O positive, because it is the most common type in the population
AB negative, because it carries both ABO antigens but not D
cards.explanation: Red cell compatibility depends on what the donor cell displays, and an O negative cell displays none of the three common antigens, so no recipient antibody has a target. Having no ABO antibodies makes AB positive the best recipient, not the best donor, because compatibility for receiving depends on plasma rather than cells. Frequency in the population affects supply but not compatibility. AB negative cells carry both ABO antigens and would be attacked by anti-A or anti-B in most recipients.

cards.q: A unit labeled B positive is accidentally started in a patient typed A positive. Trace what happens.
cards.a: The recipient's anti-B binds the donor B antigens, agglutinating and then hemolyzing the donor cells.
options: Nothing happens, because both units are Rh positive and Rh alone determines compatibility here
The recipient's anti-B binds the donor B antigens, agglutinating and hemolyzing them
The recipient's anti-A binds the donor A antigens, destroying the donor cells
The donor plasma anti-A destroys all of the recipient's red cells within seconds
cards.explanation: A type A recipient carries anti-B, the donor cells display B, and the antibody bridges them into clumps that are then lysed, releasing free hemoglobin. The recipient does not have anti-A, because they carry the A antigen themselves. Donor plasma antibodies are present in small volume and heavily diluted, so they are not the main event in a red cell transfusion reaction. Matching Rh does nothing to prevent an ABO mismatch, since the two systems are independent.

cards.q: Forward typing shows agglutination with anti-A only, but reverse typing shows the patient's plasma agglutinating known type A cells. How should this be handled?
cards.a: The two results contradict each other, so the typing must be repeated before the result is trusted.
options: The patient is type O, since reverse typing always overrules forward typing
The patient is type AB, since reacting in two different tests means both antigens are present
The two results contradict each other, so the typing must be repeated before the result is trusted
The patient is type A, and the reverse result simply confirms it
cards.explanation: Forward typing says the A antigen is present, which means the plasma should contain anti-B and not anti-A, so plasma that attacks A cells is inconsistent and points to a labeling or technique error. Calling it a confirmation misreads reverse typing, which should have been negative against A cells. Reverse typing does not automatically overrule forward typing; a discrepancy is a signal to investigate. Reacting in two tests is not evidence of two antigens when the two tests examine opposite things.

cards.q: A student records a sample as type O after seeing clumping with anti-B and no clumping with anti-A or anti-D. What is the error and the correct result?
cards.a: Clumping with anti-B means the B antigen is present, so the sample is B negative, not O.
options: No error, since type O cells clump with anti-B
The result should be O positive, since anti-B clumping indicates the D antigen
The result should be AB negative, since one positive well means both antigens
Clumping with anti-B means the B antigen is present, so the sample is B negative, not O
cards.explanation: Type O is defined by the absence of both A and B antigens, so any positive ABO well rules it out, and the lack of a reaction with anti-D makes the sample Rh negative. Type O cells carry no B antigen and cannot clump with anti-B. Anti-B detects the B antigen, not D, which has its own reagent. A single positive well shows one antigen, so AB cannot be concluded from an anti-A well that stayed negative.

cards.q: A patient types as B negative and the only units on the shelf are B positive and O positive. Explain the ABO and Rh consequences of each option.
cards.a: Neither would cause ABO agglutination, but both carry D and could sensitize this Rh negative patient to the D antigen.
options: Neither would cause ABO agglutination, but both carry D and could sensitize this patient
Both would cause immediate ABO agglutination, because the patient has anti-B
The B positive unit would agglutinate immediately, but the O positive unit would only sensitize
Neither poses any risk, because Rh incompatibility affects only pregnancy
cards.explanation: A type B recipient carries anti-A only, so B cells and O cells both pass the ABO test, but the patient lacks D and has no anti-D yet, so the risk is a delayed immune response that would make future Rh positive exposures dangerous. The patient does not have anti-B, since they carry the B antigen. The B positive unit is ABO compatible, so it would not agglutinate on those grounds. Rh sensitization from transfusion is a real problem for future transfusions as well as future pregnancies.
